attribution.note: Zitron wrote this in his own post, in his own voice.

semantics.note: It describes a current state: generative AI is attached to Search and Assistant, and users have no choice. The normalised wording 'forces' captures 'don't have a choice' fairly.

contract.note: The plain reading, 'cannot turn it off in the product', is ordinary and fair. Treating the announced Assistant-to-Gemini migration as 'stapled onto' Assistant is a little generous to the speaker, but reasonable. The March to May 2025 window is a sensible choice.

evidence.note: Google's dated Mar 2025 announcement says Assistant is being replaced by Gemini and classic Assistant will be retired. It is a company disclosure. It shows the plan, but the rollout was still under way at publication.
Google's May 20, 2025 post says Gemini powers AI Overviews in Search. This supports the AI-in-Search part. It does not address whether users could turn it off.
Reports there was no off setting, but as of May 2024. That is a different period from the target window, so it is context only.
The 'Web' filter is a per-search workaround. The contract says workarounds do not defeat the plain reading, and the report is from 2024. It does not contradict the claim.

reviews.rationale: The packet supports generative AI being built into Search (e2) and Gemini replacing Assistant (e1). The support condition also needs proof there was no AI Overviews off setting in March to May 2025. The only such evidence is from 2024, which counts as context only, and the packet itself admits the gap. Classic Assistant was also still available on many phones at publication. The 'no choice' element is therefore not settled by in-period evidence.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his post.

semantics.note: This is a causal claim that media hype, not usefulness, drove ChatGPT's growth. The add-on that OpenAI 'can't explain what it's for' is rhetorical. The normalisation is faithful.

contract.note: The contract asks for evidence that separates media exposure from usefulness as causes, which is a fair test for a causal claim. 'Useful' and 'good' are partly value judgments, and the speaker gave no measure of how much growth hype explains.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own Sept 2025 study of what people use ChatGPT for. It is a company disclosure and does not isolate the cause of growth.
OpenAI says use deepens over time among user cohorts. This is the company's own claim, gives no cohort data here, and does not control for media exposure.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no independent or causal study that separates media hype from usefulness as drivers of growth from Nov 2022 to May 2025. The OpenAI disclosures describe use, but they do not test the causal claim and they come from the company. The evidence does not settle it.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his post.

semantics.note: The normalisation keeps 'for the most part'. But the statement is a polemical characterisation of sales pitches and of Altman's motives ('manipulate, pester and terrify'), not a measurable observation. It reads as rhetoric.

contract.note: The contract rightly treats the claim as not adjudicable. There is no measurable base for 'for the most part', 'those in power' has no clear boundary, and the claim about intent is a characterisation.

evidence.note: Feb 2025 report of 400M weekly users and 2M business users, as stated by OpenAI's COO. This bears only on usage, not on how sales were pitched, so it is context.

reviews.rationale: This is a rhetorical characterisation of how AI tools are sold and of Altman's motives. No measurable base exists for 'for the most part' across all AI tools, and intent cannot be tested. The usage figures are context only.
